Imagine you have a bacterial infection, and you take an antibiotic to fight it. Most of the bacteria are killed, and you start feeling better. But here's the catch — not every bacterium is exactly the same.

## Natural Variation Is the Starting Point

Just like people in a population have slightly different traits, bacteria within a colony carry small genetic differences due to random **mutations** in their DNA. Some of these mutations happen to make a bacterium slightly less affected by a particular antibiotic. Before the antibiotic shows up, this mutation offers no special advantage, and the resistant bacterium is just one among millions.

## Selection Pressure Does the Work

When you introduce an antibiotic, you create a powerful **selection pressure**. Susceptible bacteria die off, but the few resistant individuals survive. With the competition wiped out, these survivors have abundant resources and space. They reproduce rapidly, passing the resistance gene to their offspring. Within hours or days, the population bounces back — only now it's dominated by resistant bacteria.

## It Can Spread Fast

Bacteria can also share resistance genes **horizontally** — meaning they transfer DNA directly to neighboring bacteria, even across different species, through structures like plasmids. This accelerates the problem dramatically.

## Why It Matters

This is why doctors urge you to finish your full course of antibiotics. Stopping early may kill only the weakest bacteria, leaving partially resistant ones alive to multiply. Over time, misuse and overuse of antibiotics have created dangerous "superbugs" that are extremely difficult to treat.

**Step 1: Apply the 15% discount**

After a 15% discount, the customer pays 85% of the original price:

# How a Rocket Engine Produces Thrust

A rocket engine is essentially a controlled device for throwing mass backward at very high speed. The thrust it generates follows directly from Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

## The Basic Process

Inside the engine's **combustion chamber**, propellants—a fuel and an oxidizer—are mixed and ignited. The resulting chemical reaction produces extremely hot gas at very high pressure, often exceeding 3,000°C. This gas expands rapidly and is funneled through a specially shaped **nozzle** at the base of the engine.

The nozzle is the key component. It starts narrow (the "throat") and then flares outward (the "bell"). This converging-diverging shape accelerates the gas from subsonic to supersonic speeds, converting the thermal energy of the hot gas into directed kinetic energy. The exhaust exits the nozzle at velocities of 2,000–4,500 meters per second.

## Where Thrust Comes From

By Newton's third law, as the engine pushes exhaust gas downward at tremendous speed, the gas pushes back on the engine—and therefore the rocket—with an equal force upward. You can also think of it through Newton's second law applied to momentum: the rate at which momentum is carried away by the exhaust equals the thrust force on the rocket.

Crucially, a rocket carries both its fuel *and* its oxidizer, so it doesn't need atmospheric oxygen. This is why rockets work in the vacuum of space—they push against their own exhaust, not against the air or the ground.

A rocket engine is essentially a controlled device for throwing mass in one direction so the rocket moves in the other. The underlying principle is Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

## The Basic Process

Inside the engine's **combustion chamber**, propellants—a fuel and an oxidizer—are mixed and ignited. This chemical reaction produces an enormous volume of hot, high-pressure gas. Because the chamber is sealed on all sides except one, the gas can only escape through an opening at the rear called the **nozzle**. As the gas accelerates through the nozzle and rushes out at tremendous speed (often exceeding 2–4 km/s), it carries momentum with it.

## Where the Thrust Comes From

Newton's third law tells us that the force pushing the exhaust gas backward must be matched by an equal force pushing the rocket forward. You can also think of it through Newton's second law: the engine expels mass at a high velocity, which means the exhaust carries away momentum. Since the total momentum of the system (rocket + exhaust) must be conserved, the rocket gains momentum in the opposite direction.

## Why Rockets Work in Space

Unlike a jet engine, a rocket carries its own oxidizer, so it doesn't need atmospheric air. The thrust depends only on how fast the exhaust leaves and how much mass is ejected per second. This is why rockets are the only current technology capable of operating in the vacuum of space, where there is nothing external to push against.

# Merkle Trees

A **Merkle tree** is a data structure that lets you efficiently verify the integrity of a large set of data. To understand it, let's start with the basics.

Imagine you have four chunks of data. You hash each one, producing four hashes — these form the bottom layer, or **leaves**, of the tree. Then you pair those hashes together, concatenate each pair, and hash the result, producing two new hashes — the next layer up. Finally, you combine and hash those two, producing a single hash at the top called the **Merkle root**. The result is a pyramid-shaped structure where every node is derived from the nodes below it.

## Why Is This Useful?

The Merkle root acts as a fingerprint for the *entire* dataset. If even one bit of the original data changes, the root will change completely. This property alone could be achieved by simply hashing all the data together — but the tree structure adds a crucial advantage: **efficient verification**. To prove that a specific chunk belongs to the dataset, you only need to provide a small number of hashes along the path from that chunk to the root, not the entire dataset. This is called a **Merkle proof**.

## Applications

**Git** uses Merkle trees to track the contents of a repository. Every commit, directory, and file is hashed and linked, so any change is immediately detectable and the history remains tamper-evident.

**Bitcoin** stores all transactions in a block as a Merkle tree. The root is included in the block header, allowing lightweight nodes to verify that a transaction was included without downloading every transaction in the block.

# The Attention Mechanism in Transformers

Imagine you're reading a sentence and need to understand what "it" refers to. Your brain automatically looks back at earlier words and assigns relevance to each one. Attention mechanisms formalize this intuition using linear algebra.

Given a sequence of input vectors (one per word), we create three linear projections of each vector using learned weight matrices:

- **Query (Q)**: "What am I looking for?"
- **Key (K)**: "What do I contain?"
- **Value (V)**: "What information do I carry?"

These are simply matrix multiplications: Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V, where X is your matrix of input vectors stacked as rows.

**Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k) V**

# Why Is the Sky Blue?

You already know that sunlight looks white but is actually a mix of all visible wavelengths, from red (longer waves) to violet (shorter waves). So why doesn't the sky look white—or violet, for that matter? The answer comes down to how light interacts with the atmosphere.

## Rayleigh Scattering

When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it collides with tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light. When a light wave hits one of these molecules, the molecule briefly absorbs the energy and then re-emits it in a random direction. This process is called **Rayleigh scattering**.

Here's the key: shorter wavelengths are scattered *far* more than longer ones. Specifically, the amount of scattering is proportional to 1/λ⁴ (one over the wavelength to the fourth power). That means blue light (~450 nm) is scattered roughly ten times more than red light (~700 nm). So as sunlight passes through the atmosphere, blue light gets redirected all across the sky, while red and yellow light mostly travel straight through without being disturbed.

## Why Not Violet?

Violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it's scattered even more. However, our eyes are much more sensitive to blue than to violet, and some violet light gets absorbed in the upper atmosphere. The combination means we perceive the sky as blue rather than violet.

## At Sunset

When the sun is near the horizon, its light passes through much more atmosphere. So much blue light gets scattered away that only the longer red and orange wavelengths reach your eyes directly—giving you a vivid sunset.

# How Plate Tectonics Cause Earthquakes

The Earth's outer shell isn't one solid piece. It's broken into about 15 large slabs called tectonic plates, which fit together like a cracked eggshell. These plates float on top of a layer of hot, slowly flowing rock deep beneath the surface. Heat from the Earth's core drives currents in this rock, gradually pushing the plates around — but only a few inches per year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

The problem starts where plates meet. Plates can collide head-on, pull apart from each other, or grind sideways past one another. In all three cases, the edges don't slide smoothly. Instead, the rough, jagged rock along the boundary locks together, even as the rest of each plate keeps moving. This builds up enormous stress over years or even centuries, like slowly bending a stick between your hands.

Eventually, the stress becomes too great. The locked rocks suddenly snap and lurch past each other, releasing all that stored energy in seconds. This energy radiates outward as seismic waves — vibrations that shake the ground we stand on. That shaking is what we feel as an earthquake.

This is why earthquakes concentrate along plate boundaries. The "Ring of Fire" circling the Pacific Ocean, for example, marks the edges of several major plates and produces about 90% of the world's earthquakes.

The longer a fault stays locked and the more energy it stores, the more powerful the eventual earthquake tends to be — which is what makes prediction so difficult and preparation so important.
